smell: tui.Info and tui.Warn write to stdout, not stderr. Progress/status messages belong on stderr so stdout can carry pure data. Any command piped through tools (okdctl deploy | tee log; okdctl config show > out.yaml) will mix status chatter with data. tui.Info is called 56 times across internal/cli/* on every phase including deploy, destroy, update-ingress, cleanup.
severity_reason: rubric §4/un-idiomatic-pattern: every Unix CLI convention (POSIX, clig.dev §Output, Go proverb 'be like make: noise on stderr, result on stdout') places status/log lines on stderr. Compounded because 'okdctl config show' and 'okdctl kubeconfig' do write data to stdout — mixing info on the same stream breaks piping.
fix_summary: Route tui.Info/Warn through stderrLogger. Only Print/Fprint to stdout when emitting user-requested data (config show, kubeconfig, releases list). Audit the 56 tui.Info sites — most are progress/status and belong on stderr.
rule_source: clig.dev §Output: 'Send output to stdout. Send messaging (errors, logs, info) to stderr.'
Go proverb: 'Make the zero value useful' (applies here as: stdout = data only)
repo-counter-example: internal/cli/kubeconfig.go:L69 already writes status to stderr correctly
must_preserve: tui.Error already routes to stderr — do not change. Progress bars also correctly gated on stderr TTY.

smell: README documents command/flag surface that does not exist. 'okdctl version' (line 85) is not a subcommand — only --version is wired. '--skip-terraform', '--skip-isos', '--skip-haproxy', '--skip-dns' (lines 104-105, 157) are not defined on any cobra.Command and do not appear in docs/cli/. '--remove-packages' (line 175) likewise absent.
evidence:
okdctl version          print version, git commit, build date
...
Bring your own infra
with `--skip-terraform` (existing VMs), `--skip-isos` (your own ignition),
`--skip-haproxy`, or `--skip-dns`.
...
`--remove-packages` also uninstalls `haproxy`, `dnsmasq`, `httpd`
severity_reason: rubric §4/un-idiomatic-pattern (README directs users to non-existent flags; they will see 'unknown flag' errors). Also blocks any reader who copies the Usage block verbatim.
fix_summary: Either (a) implement the missing flags: --skip-* variants on deploy (the doctor.go error message at :385 already assumes they exist), 'version' subcommand (simple alias to rootCmd.Version output), --remove-packages on destroy or cleanup; or (b) remove the stale mentions from README and docs/doctor-checks.md. doctor.go:385 reference to '--skip-* flags' also lies.
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §tooling (CI lint-yaml, no README lint)
clig.dev §Help: 'Don't document flags you don't have'
repo-counter-example: docs/cli/ shows the true flag set
must_preserve: If fix direction (a) is chosen, implementing --skip-terraform requires wiring through install.go / setup.go; out of scope for this audit.

smell: destroy uses --force/-y for skip-confirm; deploy, cleanup, update-ingress use --yes/-y. Same semantic (skip confirmation prompt), three commands use one flag name, one command uses another. Despite roadmap N11 noting the divergence is 'done', the surface is still inconsistent from a user's perspective — they must remember which command uses which name. -y is the shorthand in all four, making the long-name divergence especially confusing at --help.
evidence:
destroy.go:30:  destroyCmd.Flags().BoolVarP(&destroyForce, "force", "y", false, ...)
cleanup.go:31:  cleanupCmd.Flags().BoolVarP(&cleanupYes, "yes", "y", false, ...)
deploy.go:35:   deployCmd.Flags().BoolVarP(&deployYes, "yes", "y", false, ...)
update_ingress.go:36: updateIngressCmd.Flags().BoolVarP(&updateIngressYes, "yes", "y", false, ...)
fix_summary: Add --yes as a primary name on destroy (alongside --force for backward-compat) so the four commands have a consistent long name. Mark --force as an alias in the help text. Alternative: pick --force everywhere for destructive ops (destroy, cleanup) and --yes for non-destructive (deploy, update-ingress) — but that's a bigger split.
rule_source: clig.dev §Flags: 'Use consistent flag names for the same concept across subcommands'
repo-counter-example: three of four sibling commands already use --yes
must_preserve: --force must stay as an alias — users may have scripts relying on it.

smell: Exit code taxonomy is only partially defined. Package doc documents 0/1/2/3/4/5/130; exitCodeFor maps 4 typed errors. But (a) no code for cert-pending/recoverable; (b) SIGINT and SIGTERM collapse to 130 (143 missing); (c) cobra Args errors fall through to 1, not 64 (EX_USAGE); (d) help/--version exit status undocumented; (e) no EX_UNAVAILABLE/EX_CONFIG distinction.
fix_summary: Extend exitCodeFor: distinguish SIGTERM (143) from SIGINT (130) by checking signal.Notify receiver. Introduce BSD sysexits EX_USAGE=64 for cobra arg errors (wire via SetFlagErrorFunc or cobra.Command.Args wrapper). Add errtypes.Recoverable and errtypes.CertPending mapping if audit-errors confirms those types exist. Publish the full taxonomy as a table in docs/cli/ or a dedicated exit-codes.md.
rule_source: BSD sysexits.h: EX_USAGE=64, EX_UNAVAILABLE=69, EX_CONFIG=78
POSIX: SIGINT=128+2=130, SIGTERM=128+15=143
clig.dev §Exit codes: 'Follow a convention or document yours'
must_preserve: ConfigError=2/NetworkError=3/ClusterError=4/AuthError=5 have shipped and must stay. Backward-compatible additions only.

smell: main.go installs no signal handler. signal.NotifyContext is called inside internal/cli/root.go:execute() (line 81), which is correct placement. But preflight() at main.go:23 runs before Execute and has no cancellation — if the user hits Ctrl-C during the preflight euid check or PATH mutation, the process dies with SIGINT default (undocumented behavior, no partial summary). Low-severity because preflight is sub-millisecond in practice.
fix_summary: Either accept current behavior (documented as 'preflight is too fast to interrupt') or move signal.NotifyContext setup into main() before preflight, pass ctx through. Not worth refactoring unless preflight() grows (e.g. adds a HTTP check).
rule_source: clig.dev §Signals: 'Handle SIGINT at the earliest reasonable point'
must_preserve: preflight's 'refuse root' check must remain in main so it runs before cobra.

smell: signal.NotifyContext watches os.Interrupt AND syscall.SIGTERM, and both collapse to exit 130 at L88. 130 is SIGINT's canonical code; SIGTERM should be 143. Scripts that distinguish 'user-initiated Ctrl-C' from 'orchestrator-initiated kill' cannot tell them apart.
fix_summary: Track which signal fired via a dedicated chan. In main: chan os.Signal, buffered 1; signal.Notify(ch, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM); select on it to mark lastSig. Return 130 for Interrupt, 143 for SIGTERM. Or: document that 130 is used for both (the simpler but less POSIX-faithful option).
rule_source: POSIX exit code convention: 128+N for signal N (SIGINT=2, SIGTERM=15)
clig.dev §Signals: 'Exit code 128+N for signal N'
must_preserve: signal.NotifyContext must stay — it's how ctx cancellation propagates.

smell: Progress bar / color gating keys off stderr TTY only. Colors are rendered via lipgloss regardless of NO_COLOR env var or stdout piping. A user running 'okdctl releases list | less' gets ANSI escapes embedded in the output; 'okdctl config show > config.yaml' emits styled text into the file.
fix_summary: Add NO_COLOR respect (https://no-color.org): if os.Getenv("NO_COLOR") != "" or !term.IsTerminal(stdout.Fd()) for data-emitting commands, disable lipgloss rendering (lipgloss.SetColorProfile(termenv.Ascii)). Also add --no-color and --color=(auto|always|never) flag on rootCmd.PersistentFlags.
rule_source: NO_COLOR standard (https://no-color.org)
clig.dev §Output: 'Disable colors when !isatty(stdout)'
GNU coreutils ls convention: --color=auto|always|never
must_preserve: Progress bars already honor stderr TTY and log-format=json — keep both gates.

smell: --output json is shipped on releases list and releases show but the JSON schema is undocumented. No version field; keys follow Go struct naming via encoding/json defaults, meaning a struct rename in releases.OKDVersion ships as a schema break. No stability promise.
fix_summary: Wrap JSON output in a top-level envelope: {"schema_version": "1", "data": [...]}. Document the schema in docs/cli/json-schema.md. Freeze release.OKDVersion's JSON tags — lock fields with explicit json:"..." tags, test that Unmarshal round-trips a fixture. Note in release docs that new fields can be added; existing fields never removed or renamed without bumping schema_version.
rule_source: clig.dev §Machine-readable output: 'Document your JSON schema or users will pin on field names'
Semver §Spec for data contracts
must_preserve: Current fields must never disappear or rename — users may script against them.

smell: rootCmd.Run (line 59) prints a custom 'quick start' panel when called bare. Cobra's default for a root command with subcommands is to print --help (exit 0). The custom Run skips that, meaning 'okdctl' shows a hand-crafted landing card but not the full subcommand list. Users who run 'okdctl' bare do not see doctor, addon, releases, config, cleanup, kubeconfig, completion — 7 of 10 subcommands are hidden.
evidence:
Run: func(_ *cobra.Command, _ []string) {
    fmt.Println(tui.TitleStyle.Render("homelab k8s"))
    ...
    fmt.Println("  " + tui.HighlightStyle.Render("okdctl deploy") + "           deploy a cluster")
    fmt.Println("  " + tui.HighlightStyle.Render("okdctl destroy") + "          destroy the cluster")
    fmt.Println("  " + tui.HighlightStyle.Render("okdctl update-ingress") + "   switch ingress to loadbalancer ips")
    fmt.Println("run 'okdctl --help' for all commands")
}
fix_summary: Either (a) delete rootCmd.Run so bare invocation defers to cobra's default (prints help with all subcommands), or (b) render the quick-start card as a header prefix on the --help output via SetHelpTemplate, so users get both the curated 3 plus the full subcommand list below. (b) is the richer experience; (a) is the idiomatic minimum.
rule_source: Cobra idioms: 'Commands with subcommands should not define Run'
clig.dev §Help: 'The bare command should surface all subcommands'
must_preserve: Nothing — this Run is not load-bearing.

smell: rootCmd does not set SilenceUsage or SilenceErrors. When a RunE returns an error, cobra prints the command usage/help BEFORE the error bubbles to execute() where tui.Error renders it. Users see a 20-line usage dump for every runtime error (e.g. 'configuration file not found') — making the actual error line easy to miss.
fix_summary: Set rootCmd.SilenceUsage = true and rootCmd.SilenceErrors = true in init(). The existing tui.Error(err.Error()) at root.go:90 already renders the error — no change to user-facing error wording. Propagates to all subcommands automatically.
rule_source: Cobra FAQ §Why does cobra print usage on errors: 'Set SilenceUsage to true on your command if the error is not a usage error'
repo-counter-example: kubectl, docker, gh all set SilenceUsage
must_preserve: cobra must still print usage on cobra.Args validation failures — default behavior is correct for those; SilenceUsage only skips on RunE-returned errors.

smell: deploy ships both --non-interactive and --yes/-y as independent flags that map to the same non-interactive code path (runDeploy:40 promotes deployYes→deployNonInteractive). Two flag names for one concept is a classic anti-pattern; users now have to choose which to script against, and changing one affects the other at runtime. The --yes help text openly admits 'alias for --non-interactive', which is an argument for just making it a proper alias.
fix_summary: Collapse to one flag: keep --yes/-y as the primary name (consistent with cleanup, update-ingress), drop --non-interactive. Or: make --non-interactive a MarkHidden alias of --yes via cobra.Command.Flags().MarkHidden. The current 'both exist as siblings' is the worst option.
rule_source: clig.dev §Flags: 'Never have two flags that do the same thing'
repo-counter-example: cleanup/update-ingress use --yes alone
must_preserve: If --non-interactive has shipped, keep as hidden alias for backward-compat.

smell: README line 85 documents 'okdctl version' as a subcommand, but only --version is wired (cobra auto-flag). The subcommand form is the more discoverable one and the README promise. Also 'okdctl --version' prints the multi-line template (commit, build date, etc.) which is correct — but inconsistent with users who expect 'okdctl version' (like kubectl, docker, gh).
fix_summary: Add a versionCmd subcommand whose RunE prints the same template as --version. Register via rootCmd.AddCommand(versionCmd). Keeps --version working; satisfies 'okdctl version' expectation.
rule_source: repo-counter-example: kubectl version, docker version, gh version all exist as subcommands
README.md:85 (this repo's own docs)
must_preserve: --version flag must keep working — only add the subcommand.

smell: --output is used with two different meanings across the CLI. On deploy and kubeconfig it means 'output file path'. On releases list and releases show it means 'output format (text|json)'. Same long flag name, wildly different semantic. A user muscle-memorying 'okdctl deploy -o cfg.yaml' then typing 'okdctl releases list -o cfg.yaml' gets a schema error instead of a file.
evidence:
deploy.go:32:     StringVarP(&deployOutputFile, "output", "o", "okdctl.yaml", "output file for configuration")
kubeconfig.go:30: StringVarP(&kubeconfigOutput, "output", "o", "-", "write kubeconfig to file ('-' for stdout)")
releases.go:58:   StringVar(&releasesListOutput, "output", outputText, "output format: text|json")
releases.go:60:   StringVar(&releasesShowOutput, "output", outputText, "output format: text|json")
fix_summary: Rename the format flag on releases to --format or -F (kubectl convention), reserving --output/-o for 'where to write the output'. kubectl uses -o for format; that's a valid alternative — pick one and apply repo-wide. The breaking change on releases is low-risk (pre-1.0).
rule_source: clig.dev §Flags: 'A flag should mean the same thing everywhere'
repo-counter-example: kubectl -o is format, docker --output is file — pick one
must_preserve: releases is a read-only query — rename OK; keep deploy/kubeconfig semantics stable.

smell: deploy has no Example field on the cobra.Command. Same for destroy, cleanup, update-ingress, addon install, addon uninstall, kubeconfig, releases list, releases show, config show, config validate, doctor. Every user-facing command should have at least one concrete Example. cobra renders Examples in --help between Usage and Flags; omitting them buries the common invocations.
fix_summary:
Add Example fields. deploy: 'okdctl deploy
okdctl deploy --yes --minimal
okdctl deploy --config prod.yaml'. destroy: 'okdctl destroy
okdctl destroy --yes --keep-isos'. Similar two-to-three lines each. Auto-propagates to docs/cli/ via cobra-gen.
rule_source: Cobra docs §Examples: 'Add examples to commands'
clig.dev §Help: 'Include at least one example in help'
must_preserve: Existing Long descriptions must stay — Example is additive.

smell: promptForConfirmation writes its prompt string to os.Stdout (line 29) via _, _ = os.Stdout.WriteString(prompt). Interactive prompts belong on stderr so 'okdctl destroy | tee run.log' still lets the user see the prompt on-screen while stdout redirects cleanly.
fix_summary: Change os.Stdout.WriteString(prompt) to os.Stderr.WriteString(prompt). The prompt is a user-facing question, not data. Three callers (destroy, cleanup, update-ingress) inherit the fix.
rule_source: clig.dev §Prompts: 'Write prompts to stderr'
repo-counter-example: kubeconfig.go:69 already writes status to stderr
must_preserve: The term.IsTerminal(os.Stdin) short-circuit must stay — pre-existing N11 fix.

smell: destroy is the most dangerous verb in the CLI (tears down entire cluster + VMs). Aside from --force/-y and --keep-isos, it exposes no safety flags: no --dry-run/--plan (what would be destroyed?), no --yes-i-really-mean-it double-confirm, no --cluster-name check (typo guard: destroy mistakes another cluster's state because workdir is implicit from CWD). terraform/aws-cli conventions offer all three.
fix_summary: Add --dry-run that shells to terraform plan -destroy without apply and prints the step list without running. Add --confirm-cluster=<name> that requires the user to type the cluster name (aws-cli --yes-i-really-mean-it pattern). The double-confirm is the bigger lift; --dry-run is the minimal ask.
rule_source: clig.dev §Destructive ops: 'Double-confirm for destructive ops; offer --dry-run'
repo-counter-example: audit-state-and-recovery ux:0f076161:no-dry-run-flag (same seam)
aws-cli convention: --dry-run on all destructive verbs

smell: No --quiet/--verbose flags. --log-level is the workaround (debug/info/warn/error), but users expect -q to suppress everything except errors and -v to bump log level. --log-level exists but is less discoverable and does not short-flag. Also missing: --log-level is a persistent flag but has no -v short. Most Unix tools use -v (multiple times) for verbosity escalation.
fix_summary: Add --quiet/-q (alias for --log-level=error), --verbose/-v (alias for --log-level=debug). Keep --log-level for explicit control. The -v/-q short flags are the muscle-memory UX; --log-level is the expert knob.
rule_source: clig.dev §Flags: '-q and -v should exist on every CLI'
repo-counter-example: kubectl -v, docker --quiet, git -q

smell: addon install's Use:'install [name]' and Short:'Install one addon (or all enabled addons with --all)' imply name is optional. The Args validator actually requires exactly 1 name OR --all — neither-nor is rejected. The help text suggests you can call 'addon install' bare; the runtime says no. A user who follows the help will get 'expected exactly one addon name, or use --all' as a cobra.Args error.
fix_summary: Change Use to 'install <name> | --all' or split into install and install-all. Alternative: keep Use, change Short to 'Install <name>, or --all for all enabled'. The [name] brackets imply optional per man page conventions; replace with <name> (required notation).
rule_source: man(1) conventions: <arg> = required, [arg] = optional, | = choice
Cobra docs: 'Use parses to show argument shape'
must_preserve: Mutual-exclusion logic in Args must stay.
